The idea is wild:

☀️ Solar-powered satellites
🤖 AI chips in space
🚀 Data centers orbiting Earth
Why?
AI needs enormous amounts of electricity — and space gets almost constant sunlight.

Google’s first test is small: just four AI chips, with the system running in short bursts while engineers study heat, radiation and other space challenges.

But the long-term vision is much bigger: networks of satellites working together as an AI data center in orbit.

It sounds like science fiction.

But the first test is now scheduled for next week. 👀

Would you trust an AI running from space?

items.text:
Inference's Coming Split: Why Decode Becomes Its Own Profit Center

The standard inference stack treats prefill and decode as one pipeline with one serving configuration. That assumption is now being dismantled by two forces arriving simultaneously: the rising share of agentic workloads that stress decode more than prefill, and a new class of engines that optimize decode at a level traditional engines cannot reach.

TileRT represents the clearest expression of this shift. Its persistent kernel architecture compiles the entire decode graph into a single kernel that resides continuously on the GPU, eliminating the per-token kernel launch overhead that dominates latency at high interactivity. Verified on SemiAnalysis's InferenceX benchmark, TileRT reaches up to 500 tokens per second per user on a single B200 decode server on the GLM5 FP8 744B benchmark — approximately 3x faster than GB300 NVL72 running traditional inference engines. On AMD MI355X hardware, the AgentX benchmark measured 469 tok/s/user on GLM-5.3, more than 100 tok/s ahead of the second-place GB300 NVL72 system. At iso-cost per output token, TileRT delivers up to 2x higher interactivity.

These numbers matter because the economics of decode are structurally different from prefill. Prefill is compute-bound and bursty — the user submits a prompt, the engine computes attention across all input tokens in parallel, and the cost scales with prompt length squared. Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and long-lived — each output token requires streaming the model weights and the accumulated KV cache through the memory hierarchy. A 30B parameter model at FP16 requires 60GB of weight reads per output token. At batch size 1 on an H100 with roughly 3.35 TB/s of memory bandwidth, the theoretical ceiling is around 56 tokens per second per user. The gap between that ceiling and the roughly 500 tok/s TileRT achieves on B200 comes from a different architectural approach: TileRT's persistent kernel keeps intermediate results in registers rather than writing them back to global memory, maximizing overlap across computation, memory loads, and communication within a single kernel execution.

This creates a bifurcation in the serving stack that vLLM has now productized. vLLM's V1 connector interface allows a deployment to keep its existing prefill pool, scheduler, prefix caching, and OpenAI-compatible API surface while routing latency-critical decode traffic to a separate TileRT pool. The integration requires zero changes to the vLLM codebase — it operates entirely behind the public extensibility surface. Production deployments are already live: Xiaomi's MiMo-V2.5-Pro-UltraSpeed model exceeded 1,000 tokens per second on a 1-trillion-parameter model using a single 8-GPU node, and https://t.co/ouD5kp9EdR's GLM-5.1-HighSpeed API runs at 400 output tokens per second.

The economics of this split are where the interesting capital questions sit. Decode as a throughput commodity and decode as a latency premium are becoming distinct products. ABI Research notes that premium "fast mode" tiers typically price at 50% or more above base pricing, while offline batch inference runs at roughly a 50% discount to base mode. The same GPU running the same model can generate dramatically different revenue per GPU-hour depending on which decode engine it runs and which customer tier it serves. For inference providers operating under capacity constraints — which describes most of the market in 2026 — shifting even a fraction of high-value traffic from a throughput-optimized decode pool to a latency-optimized TileRT pool increases gross margin without additional hardware.

There is a countervailing force that deserves attention. The market assumption that a 500 tok/s target justifies buying a top-tier GPU has a flaw: we tested that claim against actual hardware economics. The consumer RTX 5090, at approximately $2,000, delivers roughly 1.79 TB/s of HBM bandwidth. For a 7-billion-parameter model at FP16, that yields a memory bandwidth roofline of approximately 240 tokens per second per user without speculative decoding or quantization — more than half the TileRT benchmark number, at one-twentieth the hardware cost. With FP4 quantization, the effective bandwidth ceiling rises further, approaching 500 tok/s. For workloads where a smaller model can deliver adequate quality, the economic argument for purchasing an 8-GPU B200 node at an estimated $400,000 or more to reach 500 tok/s collapses.

This does not invalidate TileRT's value proposition. It sharpens it. TileRT's benchmark numbers are for 744B-parameter models in FP8 — model classes that simply cannot fit on a single consumer GPU's memory, regardless of bandwidth. The premium inference market is not about running small models faster. It is about running frontier-scale models with interactive latency that was previously impossible on GPU infrastructure. The differentiation is model scale, not raw speed. A 7B model on an RTX 5090 at 240 tok/s competes with API pricing on cost, not on interactivity. A 744B model on an 8-GPU B200 node at 500 tok/s competes with Cerebras and Groq on interactivity, where the alternative is custom silicon rather than consumer hardware.

Long-context decode adds a dimension that favors the disaggregated approach. AgentX sessions routinely grow to millions of tokens. As context length increases, each generated token requires accessing an increasingly large KV cache, making memory access progressively more expensive during decode. On 8x MI350X GPUs, TileRT's single-user generation speed decreases from 648 tok/s at 1K context to 425 tok/s at 1M context — retaining roughly two-thirds of short-context performance across a 1,000x context increase. A co-located prefill and decode engine would face the same KV cache pressure while also managing prefill bursts, degrading both TTFT and inter-token latency.

The practical implication for the inference market is a three-tier structure that is already visible in pricing. Base-tier decode runs on throughput-optimized pools (vLLM native, SGLang) and serves the majority of token volume at competitive per-token pricing. Premium-tier decode runs on latency-optimized pools (TileRT, or custom silicon) and serves a smaller volume of high-value interactive traffic at 50% or more price premiums. Batch-tier inference runs offline with minimal latency requirements at roughly half the base rate. The same model, the same GPU generation, and the same cloud provider can operate across all three tiers simultaneously.

The watch item is whether this split creates durable margin expansion for inference providers or merely redistributes existing revenue. TileRT's production deployments at Xiaomi and https://t.co/ouD5kp9EdR suggest the premium tier has real demand. Whether the premium persists at scale depends on whether custom inference silicon (Cerebras, Groq, SambaNova) compresses the GPU's latency advantage before the software-layer optimization reaches broad adoption. ABI Research frames this as the central question: does TileRT represent a structural improvement in GPU economics, or a temporary software bridge before specialized decode hardware takes over?

The evidence so far favors the former. TileRT achieves its numbers without custom silicon, running on standard NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. The vLLM integration means adoption does not require rewriting the serving stack. And the production deployments are real, not pilot programs. The decode layer is becoming a distinct profit center with its own architecture, its own economics, and its own competitive dynamics — separate from the prefill commodity that the rest of the inference stack treats as undifferentiated.

Joe Lauria on Consortium News:

“Julian Assange returned to X on Thursday 25 months after being released from London’s Belmarsh Prison and eight and a half years since he last posted on the social media site.

“I’m back,” Assange posted at 9:02 a.m. EDT. 

His return comes amidst an expanding crisis of Artificial Intelligence, which captains of the AI industry have warned in recent days is slipping out of control and endangering human society.

Assange has remained away from the public since his freedom in June 2024 recovering from his five-year prison ordeal, which was preceded by seven years of confinement in the Ecuadorian embassy in London. 

He made his first post-release public appearance in Strasbourg, France on Oct. 1, 2024 at the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe’s Committee on Legal Affairs and Human Rights to discuss his case and its implications for press freedom.

“Assange next appeared at the head of a march of an estimated 300,000 people over the Sydney Harbour Bridge on Aug. 3, 2025 to protest Israel’s genocide in Gaza.  At the end of July he attended a concert in Sydney in support of pianist Jayson Gillham after the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra cancelled his 2024 concert over comments he made about journalists killed in Gaza.

“Assange’s technical expertise could put him in position to weigh in on the AI crisis. It is a non-partisan issue (https://t.co/FUAruznmm1) that lacks the controversy of comments on U.S. foreign policy.”

① Google「September 2026 Spam Update」開始

Googleは9月24日、September 2026 Spam Updateの展開を開始しました。

今回のアップデートは、

・世界全体が対象
・すべての言語が対象
・Google検索のランキングに影響
・展開完了まで最大2週間
と発表されています。
現在もアップデートは展開中です。
重要なのは、現時点でGoogleが「今回どのスパム手法を重点的に対象としているのか」を具体的に公表していないことです。

そのため、

「AI生成コンテンツが狙われている」
「寄生サイトSEOが対象」

items.text:
Inference's Coming Split: Why Decode Becomes Its Own Profit Center

The standard inference stack treats prefill and decode as one pipeline with one serving configuration. That assumption is now being dismantled by two forces arriving simultaneously: the rising share of agentic workloads that stress decode more than prefill, and a new class of engines that optimize decode at a level traditional engines cannot reach.

TileRT represents the clearest expression of this shift. Its persistent kernel architecture compiles the entire decode graph into a single kernel that resides continuously on the GPU, eliminating the per-token kernel launch overhead that dominates latency at high interactivity. Verified on SemiAnalysis's InferenceX benchmark, TileRT reaches up to 500 tokens per second per user on a single B200 decode server on the GLM5 FP8 744B benchmark — approximately 3x faster than GB300 NVL72 running traditional inference engines. On AMD MI355X hardware, the AgentX benchmark measured 469 tok/s/user on GLM-5.3, more than 100 tok/s ahead of the second-place GB300 NVL72 system. At iso-cost per output token, TileRT delivers up to 2x higher interactivity.

These numbers matter because the economics of decode are structurally different from prefill. Prefill is compute-bound and bursty — the user submits a prompt, the engine computes attention across all input tokens in parallel, and the cost scales with prompt length squared. Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and long-lived — each output token requires streaming the model weights and the accumulated KV cache through the memory hierarchy. A 30B parameter model at FP16 requires 60GB of weight reads per output token. At batch size 1 on an H100 with roughly 3.35 TB/s of memory bandwidth, the theoretical ceiling is around 56 tokens per second per user. The gap between that ceiling and the roughly 500 tok/s TileRT achieves on B200 comes from a different architectural approach: TileRT's persistent kernel keeps intermediate results in registers rather than writing them back to global memory, maximizing overlap across computation, memory loads, and communication within a single kernel execution.

This creates a bifurcation in the serving stack that vLLM has now productized. vLLM's V1 connector interface allows a deployment to keep its existing prefill pool, scheduler, prefix caching, and OpenAI-compatible API surface while routing latency-critical decode traffic to a separate TileRT pool. The integration requires zero changes to the vLLM codebase — it operates entirely behind the public extensibility surface. Production deployments are already live: Xiaomi's MiMo-V2.5-Pro-UltraSpeed model exceeded 1,000 tokens per second on a 1-trillion-parameter model using a single 8-GPU node, and https://t.co/ouD5kp9EdR's GLM-5.1-HighSpeed API runs at 400 output tokens per second.

The economics of this split are where the interesting capital questions sit. Decode as a throughput commodity and decode as a latency premium are becoming distinct products. ABI Research notes that premium "fast mode" tiers typically price at 50% or more above base pricing, while offline batch inference runs at roughly a 50% discount to base mode. The same GPU running the same model can generate dramatically different revenue per GPU-hour depending on which decode engine it runs and which customer tier it serves. For inference providers operating under capacity constraints — which describes most of the market in 2026 — shifting even a fraction of high-value traffic from a throughput-optimized decode pool to a latency-optimized TileRT pool increases gross margin without additional hardware.

There is a countervailing force that deserves attention. The market assumption that a 500 tok/s target justifies buying a top-tier GPU has a flaw: we tested that claim against actual hardware economics. The consumer RTX 5090, at approximately $2,000, delivers roughly 1.79 TB/s of HBM bandwidth. For a 7-billion-parameter model at FP16, that yields a memory bandwidth roofline of approximately 240 tokens per second per user without speculative decoding or quantization — more than half the TileRT benchmark number, at one-twentieth the hardware cost. With FP4 quantization, the effective bandwidth ceiling rises further, approaching 500 tok/s. For workloads where a smaller model can deliver adequate quality, the economic argument for purchasing an 8-GPU B200 node at an estimated $400,000 or more to reach 500 tok/s collapses.

This does not invalidate TileRT's value proposition. It sharpens it. TileRT's benchmark numbers are for 744B-parameter models in FP8 — model classes that simply cannot fit on a single consumer GPU's memory, regardless of bandwidth. The premium inference market is not about running small models faster. It is about running frontier-scale models with interactive latency that was previously impossible on GPU infrastructure. The differentiation is model scale, not raw speed. A 7B model on an RTX 5090 at 240 tok/s competes with API pricing on cost, not on interactivity. A 744B model on an 8-GPU B200 node at 500 tok/s competes with Cerebras and Groq on interactivity, where the alternative is custom silicon rather than consumer hardware.

Long-context decode adds a dimension that favors the disaggregated approach. AgentX sessions routinely grow to millions of tokens. As context length increases, each generated token requires accessing an increasingly large KV cache, making memory access progressively more expensive during decode. On 8x MI350X GPUs, TileRT's single-user generation speed decreases from 648 tok/s at 1K context to 425 tok/s at 1M context — retaining roughly two-thirds of short-context performance across a 1,000x context increase. A co-located prefill and decode engine would face the same KV cache pressure while also managing prefill bursts, degrading both TTFT and inter-token latency.

The practical implication for the inference market is a three-tier structure that is already visible in pricing. Base-tier decode runs on throughput-optimized pools (vLLM native, SGLang) and serves the majority of token volume at competitive per-token pricing. Premium-tier decode runs on latency-optimized pools (TileRT, or custom silicon) and serves a smaller volume of high-value interactive traffic at 50% or more price premiums. Batch-tier inference runs offline with minimal latency requirements at roughly half the base rate. The same model, the same GPU generation, and the same cloud provider can operate across all three tiers simultaneously.

The watch item is whether this split creates durable margin expansion for inference providers or merely redistributes existing revenue. TileRT's production deployments at Xiaomi and https://t.co/ouD5kp9EdR suggest the premium tier has real demand. Whether the premium persists at scale depends on whether custom inference silicon (Cerebras, Groq, SambaNova) compresses the GPU's latency advantage before the software-layer optimization reaches broad adoption. ABI Research frames this as the central question: does TileRT represent a structural improvement in GPU economics, or a temporary software bridge before specialized decode hardware takes over?

The evidence so far favors the former. TileRT achieves its numbers without custom silicon, running on standard NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. The vLLM integration means adoption does not require rewriting the serving stack. And the production deployments are real, not pilot programs. The decode layer is becoming a distinct profit center with its own architecture, its own economics, and its own competitive dynamics — separate from the prefill commodity that the rest of the inference stack treats as undifferentiated.

Your coding agent can remember a rule — and still miss it when a write is about to happen.

Writ is a governance runtime for Claude Code that helps engineers put selected workflow controls outside model context.

It helps you make plan and test checkpoints enforceable during implementation by running configured boundaries at tool time, rather than relying only on the agent to follow instructions.

Key features:

• Tool-time write gates – in Work mode, source-code writes are blocked until plan and test gates are approved
• Relevant rule delivery – rules are selected by task, file, tool, and workflow phase
• Session modes – supports conversation, review, investigate, debug, and work modes
• Decision provenance – connects approved plans, governing rule IDs, changed files, and commits
• Local rulebook – uses a Neo4j-backed knowledge graph to retrieve applicable engineering rules

It’s open-source (MIT license).

Google’s rapid iteration continues. The new 3.8 Flash is optimized for "agentic loops," showing a massive jump in terminal-based benchmarks (90.8%). It also introduces the Flash Cyber variant, specifically tuned for automated vulnerability patching and security defense.

The focus has shifted from making models smarter to making them more reliable—reducing tool-call errors, managing context memory more efficiently (DeepSeek), and improving agentic "self-correction" (Meta).

Today we’re launching our leaderboard for Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, an agentic benchmark for scientific research work. GPT-6 Astra (max) and Claude Opus 5.5 (xhigh) currently top it at 63% and 62%

Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 was announced in August 2026, built by @StevenDillmann and researchers at Stanford with the @terminalbench team and a global community of open source scientific contributors. It has 70 expert-curated tasks based on real research in five domains: life sciences (19), physical sciences (17), mathematical sciences (17), engineering sciences (9), and earth sciences (8).

As with Terminal-Bench, each task drops an agent into a sandbox environment with the data, tools and instructions for a task, and the agent runs from start to finish. Automated tests grade every task pass/fail, and we report the average pass@1 over 3 attempts.

Key takeaways:

➤ Only two models score above 50%: GPT-6 Astra (max) at 63%, and Claude Opus 5.5 at 62% (xhigh) and 59% (max). Recent releases have made large advancements, but even the top model, GPT-6 Astra, has significant headroom

➤ Life sciences is the lowest-scoring domain for most leading models, though domain scores are noisy with 8 to 19 tasks each. Claude Opus 5.5 (xhigh) passes 71% of mathematical sciences tasks but 46% of life sciences tasks

➤ The best open weights models, GLM-5.3 (max) at 10% and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max) at 9%, sit more than 50 points below the leaders
